# Spring Boot Web Application using Project Leyden AOT Cache

Project Leyden aims to improve Java startup time, time to peak performance, and
footprint by shifting selected work earlier in time. A working Spring Boot image
alone does not show whether an AOT cache was created and used. This example
compares local launches with and without the cache, then builds an image that
creates and uses its own cache.

This module uses the same Spring Boot quote application used by the other Spring
Boot examples in this workshop. The application is intentionally unchanged so
that the reader can focus on the JVM packaging and startup behaviour.

This focused example does not cover every aspect of running Java in containers.
It omits some production-oriented container concerns, such as running as a
non-root user, image signing, vulnerability scanning, observability, and
deployment-specific hardening, so the AOT cache behaviour remains easy to
follow. For a more complete Spring Boot container example that combines several
concerns, see
[all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).

This example teaches the Leyden AOT cache workflow:

- Train the JVM through the application context refresh.
- Create an AOT cache from that launch.
- Run the same application with the cache.
- Package the cache in a container image built and run with the same JDK build.

A useful way to compare CDS and the Leyden AOT cache is to look at the work the
JVM normally performs during startup:

```text
class file on disk
  -> read and parsed
  -> metadata created
  -> class loaded
  -> class linked
  -> class initialized
  -> methods interpreted or JIT compiled
```

CDS stores preprocessed class metadata in an archive that the JVM can map at
startup instead of reading and parsing the same class files again. AppCDS
extends that idea from JDK classes to application and dependency classes. The
Leyden AOT cache builds on this foundation, but it is not just AppCDS with a new
name: it can also preserve later class-processing work, especially loading and
linking, so classes can be available in a loaded and linked state when the JVM
starts.

Creating either archive involves a prior training run; using one does not resume
that process. The production JVM still starts a new application under normal
Java runtime rules. This also differs from compiling the whole application into
a native executable.

An AOT cache uses CDS mechanisms and includes cached class data. It replaces the
separate AppCDS archive for this application workflow. A custom runtime may
contain a CDS archive generated by `jlink`, but that file’s presence does not
establish that it is mapped when the application selects an explicit AOT cache;
inspect the JVM logs for the actual launch configuration. For Spring Boot on
Java 25, the AOT cache is the recommended application startup workflow; CDS
remains relevant to Java 21 deployments and to explaining what the cache builds
on.

## Learning objectives

By the end of this example, attendees can:

- inspect how the Dockerfile creates and packages an AOT cache;
- build an executable JAR and prepare a consistent explicit class path;
- compare observed startup times with and without the cache; and
- explain why cache compatibility and representative training matter in a
  container image.

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- `jar` included with a full JDK installation.

- [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) runtime

- `curl`, `jq`, and `tree`

- A POSIX-compatible shell with `find`, `sort`, `paste`, `grep`, `rm`, and `kill`
  available on the `PATH` for the local class path workflow.

The JDK, Docker, and command-line utilities checked above are required for
the walkthrough; no separate inspection tool is optional.

## The artefacts to inspect

The Spring Boot quote application serves `/quote/random` and packages its
classes, resources, and dependencies into an executable JAR. The build creates
`target/leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar`; both the local class path
launch and the image build start from that same JAR.

Inspect `containers/Dockerfile` before building the image. Its builder stage
extracts the JAR, writes a stable class path to `java.args`, and creates
`app.aot`. The final stage copies the application JAR, dependencies, argument
file, and cache into the runtime image. Its entry point reuses `java.args` so
the launch has the same class path order as cache creation.

```dockerfile
FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1 AS builder
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

ARG JAR_FILE="./target/leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot-*.jar"
COPY ["${JAR_FILE}", "app.jar"]

# The AOT cache is tied to the exact class path used during training. Even a
# different dependency JAR order invalidates the cache, so write the class path
# to java.args and use that same argument file for cache creation and startup.
RUN mkdir "extracted" \
    && (cd "extracted" && jar -xf "../app.jar") \
    && jar --create --file "application.jar" -C "extracted/BOOT-INF/classes" "." \
    && printf '%s\n' "--class-path" "application.jar:$(find "extracted/BOOT-INF/lib" -type f -name '*.jar' | sort | paste -sd ":" -)" "demo.Main" > "java.args" \
    && java \
        -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh \
        -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot \
        @java.args

FROM container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1
WORKDIR "/opt/app"

COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib", "./extracted/BOOT-INF/lib"]
COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/application.jar", "./application.jar"]
COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/java.args", "./java.args"]
COPY --from=builder ["/opt/app/app.aot", "./app.aot"]

ENV JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-XX:AOTCache=app.aot -XX:AOTMode=on"

EXPOSE 8080

# Reuse java.args so runtime sees the same class path order used to create the
# AOT cache.
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "@java.args"]
```

## Build the application

The application is built once and then reused for the local runtime checks and
the container image. This matters because the comparison should isolate the
runtime packaging choice, not a different application build. The first launch is
a sanity check for the executable Spring Boot JAR; the measured Leyden
comparison happens later, after the application is converted to the same
explicit class path used for AOT cache creation and cache reuse.

1. Build the application.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

## Guided walkthrough

Run the following commands from `examples/leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot`. The
local runs use port 8080 in sequence; stop each process before starting the next
one. The startup times are observations from this environment, not portable
benchmarks.

1. Run the executable JAR as a baseline.

   This confirms that the packaged JAR works before the container steps add
   Dockerfiles and image layers to the picture.

   The application is started in the background for convenience, otherwise the
   subsequent commands need to be executed in another terminal.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   (*Optional*) Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Margaret Thatcher",
     "id": 116,
     "quote": "What is success? I think it is a mixture of having a flair for the thing that you are doing; knowing that it is not enough, that you have got to have hard work and a certain sense of purpose."
   }
   ```

2. Read the startup time.

   ```shell
   grep 'Started Main in' './target/output.txt'
   ```

   The application startup time

   ```
   2077-04-27T11:34:56.789Z  INFO 188852 --- [           main] demo.Main                                : Started Main in 3.043 seconds (process running for 3.382)
   ```

3. Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

4. Record the executable JAR baseline.

   | Application    |   Start up Time |
   | -------------- | --------------: |
   | Executable JAR | `3.043` seconds |

This is a useful smoke-test baseline, but it is not yet the best comparison for
Leyden. The executable JAR uses Spring Boot’s launcher and nested JAR class
loading, while the AOT cache commands below use an explicit class path. To make
the AOT comparison fair, measure the explicit class path without a cache first
and then run the same launch again with the cache enabled.

### Prepare a class path launch

Spring Boot executable JARs use the Spring Boot launcher and nested JAR support.
That is convenient for deployment, but it hides application and dependency
classes behind a launcher-specific class loading arrangement. For this Leyden
example, extract the archive and run the application from a regular class path.
That gives the training run, the baseline launch, and the cached launch the same
application JAR, dependency JARs, main class, and class path order.

1. Extract the Spring Boot archive.

   ```shell
   rm -rf './target/extracted' './target/application.jar'
   mkdir -p './target/extracted'
   (cd './target/extracted'
    jar -xf '../leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar')
   ```

2. Package the application classes and resources into a normal JAR.

   ```shell
   jar --create \
     --file './target/application.jar' \
     -C './target/extracted/BOOT-INF/classes' .
   ```

   Spring Boot also leaves the original Maven JAR at
   `target/leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original`. That file could be
   used as the application JAR because it contains the application classes and
   resources before Spring Boot repackages the archive. This runbook creates
   `target/application.jar` from `BOOT-INF/classes` instead so the layout is
   explicit: one normal JAR for this application, plus the dependency JARs from
   `BOOT-INF/lib`.

   AOT cache validity depends on the runtime inputs staying consistent. To make
   that consistency explicit, write the class path and main class to
   `target/java.args` and reuse the same argument file for the baseline launch,
   cache creation, and cached launch.

3. Create the Java argument file.

   The AOT cache records the class path used during training. Even a different
   dependency JAR order can make the cache unusable, so the dependency JARs are
   sorted once and written to `target/java.args`.

   ```shell
   printf '%s\n' \
     '--class-path' \
     "./target/application.jar:$(find './target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib' -type f -name '*.jar' | sort | paste -sd ':' -)" \
     'demo.Main' > './target/java.args'
   ```

4. Run the application from the extracted class path without an AOT cache.

   This is the main local baseline for the Leyden experiment. It uses the same
   class path and main class as the cached run, but without `-XX:AOTCache`.

   ```shell
   java '@./target/java.args' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Voltaire",
     "id": 171,
     "quote": "Every man is guilty of all the good he did not do."
   }
   ```

   A successful response confirms that the application works with the new
   packaging layout. The next command reads the no-cache startup time used in
   the later AOT comparison.

5. Read the class path startup time.

   ```shell
   grep 'Started Main in' './target/output.txt'
   ```

   The no-cache class path startup time.

   ```
   2077-04-27T11:35:01.034Z  INFO 189155 --- [           main] demo.Main                                : Started Main in 2.477 seconds (process running for 2.704)
   ```

6. Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

7. Analyse the local baselines.

   | Application                   |   Start up Time |
   | ----------------------------- | --------------: |
   | Executable Spring Boot JAR    | `3.043` seconds |
   | Explicit class path, no cache | `2.477` seconds |

   The explicit class path launch may already be faster than the executable JAR.
   That is not a Leyden result yet. The executable JAR uses Spring Boot’s
   launcher, nested JAR handling, and a launcher-specific class loader. The
   explicit class path launch gives the JVM normal JAR files directly, so there
   is less launcher and nested-archive work during startup.

   There is also a measurement-order effect: the second run can benefit from the
   operating system’s file cache because the same application and dependency
   JARs were just read by the previous launch. Treat this table as packaging
   context. The Leyden comparison starts with the explicit class path, no-cache
   row and compares it with the same explicit class path plus `-XX:AOTCache`.

### Create the AOT cache

JDK 25 adds `-XX:AOTCacheOutput`, which performs the training run and creates
the cache in one command for common cases. The Spring property
`spring.context.exit=onRefresh` lets the training run build the application
context and then exit without leaving the HTTP server running. That is the
behaviour we want for startup training: the JVM sees the classes, resources, and
framework paths needed to refresh the Spring context, but the command still
finishes as a build step.

AOT cache training is workload-sensitive. If your real application performs
important lazy initialisation only after the first HTTP request, this
`onRefresh` training run will not cover that later path. Java 25 can also record
method profiles in the cache; a context-refresh-only run does not exercise
request-handling methods for that purpose. This example isolates startup, so it
deliberately uses the shorter training run.

1. Create the cache.

   The cache is created as a single file: `./target/app.aot`. This command uses
   `@./target/java.args` so the training run uses the same class path and main
   class as the later baseline and cached launches.

   ```shell
   rm -f './target/app.aot'
   java \
     -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh \
     -XX:AOTCacheOutput='./target/app.aot' \
     @./target/java.args > './target/aot-create-output.txt' 2>&1
   ```

   `-XX:AOTCacheOutput` is a convenience option. It first runs the application
   in a training mode, records an intermediate AOT configuration, and then
   starts a second JVM to create the cache. That child JVM receives the required
   options through `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`, so the output can include a long line
   beginning with `Picked up JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS`. The long value is mostly the
   class path from `target/java.args`; it is expected and can be ignored when
   reading the runbook output.

2. Confirm that the cache was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -P 'app.aot*' --prune './target'
   ```

   The cache file.

   ```
   ./target
   └── app.aot

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

3. Inspect the training output.

   ```shell
   grep -E 'AOTConfiguration|AOTCache creation is complete|Started Main in' \
     './target/aot-create-output.txt'
   ```

   The training output.

   ```
   Temporary AOTConfiguration recorded: ./target/app.aot.config

-Djava.class.path=./target/application.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/angus-activation-2.0.3.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/antlr4-runtime-4.13.2.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/aspectjweaver-1.9.25.1.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/byte-buddy-1.18.11.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/commons-logging-1.3.6.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/error_prone_annotations-2.50.0.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/failureaccess-1.0.3.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/flyway-core-12.4.0.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/guava-33.7.2-jre.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/h2-2.4.240.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/hibernate-core-7.4.5.Final.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/hibernate-models-1.1.1.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/HikariCP-7.0.2.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/istack-commons-runtime-4.1.2.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/j2objc-annotations-3.1.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jackson-annotations-2.21.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jackson-core-3.1.5.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jackson-databind-3.1.5.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jakarta.activation-api-2.1.4.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jakarta.annotation-api-3.0.0.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jakarta.inject-api-2.0.1.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jakarta.persistence-api-3.2.0.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jakarta.transaction-api-2.0.1.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jakarta.xml.bind-api-4.0.5.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jaxb-core-4.0.9.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jaxb-runtime-4.0.9.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jboss-logging-3.6.3.Final.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jspecify-1.0.1.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/jul-to-slf4j-2.0.18.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/listenablefuture-9999.0-empty-to-avoid-conflict-with-guava.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/log4j-api-2.25.5.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/log4j-to-slf4j-2.25.5.jar:./target/extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/logback-classic-1.    AOTCache creation is complete: ./target/app.aot 110551040 bytes

   (*Optional*) Explicit record/create workflow.

   The command above uses the JDK 25 convenience option `-XX:AOTCacheOutput`.
   Earlier Leyden builds, and some advanced workflows, use the explicit two-step
   form shown below. The first JVM records an AOT configuration in
   `app.aotconf`. The second JVM reads that configuration and creates `app.aot`.
   You usually do not need this form unless the training run and cache creation
   need to happen as separate steps.

   ```shell
   rm -f './target/app.aotconf' \
         './target/app.aot' \
         './target/aot-record-output.txt' \
         './target/aot-create-output.txt'

   java \
     -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh \
     -XX:AOTMode=record \
     -XX:AOTConfiguration='./target/app.aotconf' \
     @./target/java.args > './target/aot-record-output.txt' 2>&1

   java \
     -XX:AOTMode=create \
     -XX:AOTConfiguration='./target/app.aotconf' \
     -XX:AOTCache='./target/app.aot' \
     @./target/java.args > './target/aot-create-output.txt' 2>&1
   ```

   If you run the explicit workflow, confirm that it produced both the
   configuration and the cache.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -P 'app.aot*' --prune './target'
   ```

   The configuration and cache files.

   ```
   ./target
   ├── app.aot
   └── app.aotconf

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

   Inspect the cache creation output. The `create` step should show that the JVM
   read `./target/app.aotconf` and wrote `./target/app.aot`. The most important
   line is `AOTCache creation is complete`, followed by the cache path and size.

   ```shell
   grep -E 'Reading AOTConfiguration|AOTCache creation is complete|AOT' \
     './target/aot-create-output.txt' | head
   ```

   The AOT cache creation.

   ```
   Reading AOTConfiguration ./target/app.aotconf and writing AOTCache ./target/app.aot
   [0.629s][warning][aot] Skipping org/springframework/core/ReactiveAdapterRegistry$ReactorAdapter: Unlinked class not supported by AOTClassLinking
   [0.629s][warning][aot] Skipping org/springframework/web/servlet/view/freemarker/FreeMarkerView: Unlinked class not supported by AOTClassLinking
   [0.630s][warning][aot] Skipping org/springframework/boot/logging/log4j2/Log4J2LoggingSystem: Unlinked class not supported by AOTClassLinking
   AOTCache creation is complete: ./target/app.aot 110567424 bytes
   ```

   You may also see AOT warnings about skipped classes, failed verification, or
   unsupported generated/proxy classes. Those warnings are common with framework
   applications such as Spring Boot. They mean those particular classes were not
   archived, not that the whole cache failed. Treat the cache creation as
   successful when the command exits successfully and reports that the AOT cache
   creation is complete.

### Run with the AOT cache

Now run the same explicit class path launch, but pass the AOT cache created in
the previous section. This checks two things: the cache is compatible with the
current JVM and class path, and the application still behaves normally when the
JVM starts with cached class-loading and linking information. Compare this
result with the explicit class path baseline, not only with the executable JAR
smoke test, because that keeps the launch shape constant.

1. Start the application with the cache.

   This launch reuses `@./target/java.args`, so the runtime class path and main
   class match the training run that created `./target/app.aot`.

   ```shell
   java \
     -XX:AOTCache='./target/app.aot' \
     -XX:AOTMode=on \
     @./target/java.args > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   `-XX:AOTMode=on` is useful while learning because it makes cache use
   mandatory. If the JVM cannot use the cache, the application launch fails
   instead of silently continuing without it. That makes configuration mistakes
   visible, such as using a cache created with a different JDK build, operating
   system, architecture, class path, module options, or application artefact.

   Without `-XX:AOTMode=on`, the JVM can fall back to a normal startup when the
   cache is missing or unusable. That fallback is usually the better production
   default: the application still starts, but it may lose the startup benefit
   expected from the AOT cache. Use the mandatory mode only when a stale or
   invalid cache should be treated as a deployment error.

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Winston Churchill",
     "id": 193,
     "quote": "We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give."
   }
   ```

2. Read the startup time.

   ```shell
   grep 'Started Main in' './target/output.txt'
   ```

   The application start time.

   ```
   2077-04-27T11:35:23.809Z  INFO 189597 --- [           main] demo.Main                                : Started Main in 0.768 seconds (process running for 0.98)
   ```

3. Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

4. Analyse the local AOT result.

   | Application                    |   Start up Time |
   | ------------------------------ | --------------: |
   | Executable Spring Boot JAR     | `3.043` seconds |
   | Explicit class path, no cache  | `2.477` seconds |
   | Explicit class path, AOT cache | `0.768` seconds |

   The important comparison is between the second and third rows. Both launches
   use the same application JAR, dependency JARs, main class, and class path;
   the third launch adds only the AOT cache. If the cached run is faster, the
   result is consistent with the JVM reusing work captured during training,
   including class loading and linking. These single runs do not establish a
   repeatable performance gain.

   Do not compare the third row only with the executable JAR row. That would mix
   two changes at once: Spring Boot’s executable JAR launcher versus the
   explicit class path, and no AOT cache versus the AOT cache.

### Container image

The AOT cache is specific to the JDK release, operating system, architecture,
module options, and class path used to create it. For containers, create the
cache in the image build using the same JDK build as the final image. Do not
copy the cache produced on the host into the image unless the host and image
runtime are deliberately matched. Building the cache inside the container image
keeps the training JVM and the final runtime JVM aligned.

Class path order matters too. The AOT cache records the class path used during
training, and the runtime launch must use the same entries in the same order.
The Dockerfile therefore writes the sorted class path to `java.args` during the
builder stage and reuses that same argument file in the final image. Do not
replace it with `extracted/BOOT-INF/lib/*` in the final `ENTRYPOINT`; wildcard
expansion can produce a different JAR order and make the JVM reject the cache.

1. Build the container image.

   The Dockerfile repeats the same extraction and explicit class path layout
   used locally. During the builder stage, it runs the application with
   `-Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh` and `-XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot`, then
   copies the application JAR, dependency JARs, generated cache, and `java.args`
   argument file into the runtime stage.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
     --tag 'leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot:latest' \
     .
   ```

2. Run the container.

   ```shell
   docker run \
     --rm \
     --detach \
     --publish '8080:8080' \
     --name 'leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot' \
     'leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot:latest'
   ```

   Wait for the container to start.

   ```shell
   until curl --silent --fail 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' >/dev/null; do sleep 1; done
   ```

   Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "Aristotle",
     "id": 19,
     "quote": "Courage is the first of human qualities because it is the quality which guarantees the others."
   }
   ```

3. Read the container startup time.

   ```shell
   docker logs 'leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot' | grep 'Started Main in'
   ```

   The container startup time.

   ```
   2077-04-27T11:35:43.590Z  INFO 1 --- [           main] demo.Main                                : Started Main in 0.922 seconds (process running for 1.167)
   NOTE: Picked up JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS: -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -XX:AOTMode=on
   ```

   4. Stop the application.

   ```shell
   docker stop 'leyden-aot-cache-spring-boot'
   ```

5. Analyse the results.

   | Application                    |   Start up Time |
   | ------------------------------ | --------------: |
   | Executable Spring Boot JAR     | `3.043` seconds |
   | Explicit class path, no cache  | `2.477` seconds |
   | Explicit class path, AOT cache | `0.768` seconds |
   | Container with AOT cache       | `0.922` seconds |

   Treat these numbers as local observations, not portable benchmarks. The most
   useful local comparison is the direction and magnitude between the explicit
   class path baseline and the explicit class path AOT cache run. The container
   number proves that the cache can be packaged with the application, but it is
   still not an apples-to-apples measurement against the non-container JVM runs,
   even when every command is executed on the same VM.

   The value captured from `docker logs` is still Spring Boot’s in-process
   startup time; it does not include the time Docker needs to create the
   container, attach networking, or publish the port. If the container row is
   considerably slower, the likely causes are the runtime environment rather
   than the `docker run` command itself. A containerized JVM can see different
   CPU and memory limits through cgroups, read classes and the AOT cache through
   the image filesystem rather than the local `target` directory, and run with a
   different Linux userspace than the non-container JVM process. On a small VM,
   memory pressure and disk throughput can make those differences more visible.

   The runtime image sets both `-XX:AOTCache=app.aot` and `-XX:AOTMode=on`. The
   mandatory mode is intentional for the workshop: if the cache cannot be used,
   the container should fail instead of silently falling back to a normal
   startup and making the result look like a slow cached run. One common cause
   of failure is a class path mismatch, for example when the cache was created
   with one dependency JAR order but the runtime launch expands `BOOT-INF/lib/*`
   in another order.

   This comparison checks whether the cached run is faster, but it also
   reinforces what makes the cache valid:

   - Same JDK release and compatible runtime image.
   - Same operating system and hardware architecture.
   - Consistent class path and module options.
   - Training run that reaches the startup paths the production launch needs.

   If the training run is too shallow, the application still works, but the
   cache will cover less startup work.

## References

- [JEP 483: Ahead-of-Time Class Loading & Linking](https://openjdk.org/jeps/483)
- [JEP 514: Ahead-of-Time Command-Line Ergonomics](https://openjdk.org/jeps/514)
- [JEP 515: Ahead-of-Time Method Profiling](https://openjdk.org/jeps/515)
- [Java Virtual Machine Guide: Class Data Sharing](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/vm/class-data-sharing.html)
- [Spring Boot: AOT Cache](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/packaging/aot-cache.html)

## Key takeaways and trade-offs

- The Java 25 AOT cache includes CDS class data, so this workflow needs no
  separate AppCDS archive. The explicit class path runs make the local no-cache
  and cached launches comparable.
- The image builds the cache with its own JDK and reuses the recorded class path
  at launch.
- Training only through Spring context refresh can miss work deferred until a
  request or later application activity.
- Startup times depend on the host and container environment. Decide whether a
  mandatory cache or a fallback launch suits the deployment.
